core_claim: USF-Audio expands digital audio dynamic range by folding signals before digitization and mathematically reconstructing the original waveform.
topic: A research prototype uses analog waveform folding and mathematical reconstruction to capture greater audio dynamic range within a six-bit converter.
title: How Digital Audio Can Capture More Dynamic Range
hook: Can six bits preserve quiet and loud sounds?
description:
Imperial College London researchers demonstrated USF-Audio, a research-stage audio capture method that folds a waveform before digitization and mathematically reconstructs it. A six-bit prototype achieved at least 18 dB more dynamic range than a conventional six-bit converter. In a 52-person listening study, reconstructed audio received higher quality ratings. This is a research prototype, not a consumer recorder product.

Research: Imperial College London — https://www.imperial.ac.uk/news/articles/2026/imperial-engineers-challenge-90-year-limitation-in-digital-audio-sensing/
Independent analysis: XenoSpectrum — https://xenospectrum.com/en/usf-audio-modulo-wrapping-adc/
cover_payoff: Use an original short violin phrase as an audio illustration while a quiet-to-loud waveform is shown being folded, digitized and reconstructed. Use the pinned CC0 sample source; no creator performance recording is included, so do not describe this as Prince's live performance.
narration_script: Digital audio research is challenging an old limit. Researchers fold the signal before digitizing, then mathematically reconstruct its original waveform. The six-bit prototype achieved at least eighteen decibels greater dynamic range. Fifty-two listeners rated reconstructed audio quality higher than conventional recordings.

narration_evidence.quote: A research team at Imperial College London, made up of Ruiming Guo, Yuliang Zhu and Ayush Bhandari, has developed USF-Audio, a new technique that folds an audio waveform before digitizing it and then mathematically reconstructs the original waveform afterward.
In experiments using just six bits per sample, the prototype achieved at least 18 dB greater dynamic range than a conventional six-bit converter.
A listening study involving 52 participants also found that reconstructed audio received higher quality ratings than conventional recordings at the same bit depth.
